extracted.intended_audience: NLP and ML researchers working on patent analysis, generation, and multimodal patent processing
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive survey summarizing the characteristics of patent documents, patent-related NLP tasks (analysis and generation), datasets, methods (including LLMs and multimodal), evaluation metrics, and research challenges to guide NLP researchers working on patent-domain problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable a technical solution must be (1) new, (2) involve an inventive step (non-obviousness), and (3) be industrially applicable (utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are substantive legal prerequisites checked during examination; novelty is assessed against all prior art, inventive step compares to the state of the art, and utility/industrial applicability can be less strictly commercial but must show basic feasibility. Datasets or labelling heuristics that infer novelty (e.g., award-linked patents or cross-office rejection) may deviate from this formal definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent document structural elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents normally include publication information, title, bibliometric information (applicants, inventors, assignees, examiners, attorneys), classification codes, citations/prior art, abstract, background, detailed description, claims, and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each section has a distinct role: abstracts are brief and generic; descriptions contain comprehensive embodiments and are information-rich; claims define the legal scope; drawings support but do not replace text. For NLP tasks, segmentation into these sections is a common preprocessing step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims drafting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the legal scope of the patent; each claim is typically a single sentence and describes invention features that establish novelty and non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be precise, carefully worded to delineate scope and withstand legal scrutiny. For generation tasks, ensuring claims adhere to single-sentence structure, consistent terminology, and legal precision is critical. Keystroke-based metrics have been proposed to evaluate claim-autocompletion utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new matter in amendments (preserve priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments must not introduce novel features (inventive content) that extend beyond the original filing; otherwise they may lose the original date stamp or be rejected/ challenged later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When generating or editing patent text, do not add new inventive content post-filing; dataset creation and model evaluation must respect this constraint when simulating drafting or amendment scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology consistency and precision requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent texts demand extremely high precision and consistent use of terminology; a technical term must not be replaced by other words unless explicitly equated in the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High information density leads to repetitiveness and long, clause-laden sentences. LLMs prone to paraphrase or synonym-substitution can violate consistency, producing legally harmful drift. Models and evaluation should measure fidelity to original terminology and clarity of scopes (PatentEval highlights error types like irrelevant content and incomplete coverage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long context handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent descriptions are often very long (average description token counts can exceed 11,000 tokens), exceeding many LLMs' context windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For analysis and generation, models must handle long-range dependencies; use long-context LLMs, sparse/structured attention (e.g., BigBird, Longformer), or segmentation strategies. Avoid relying solely on titles/abstracts—the description and claims contain crucial details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical and domain-specific language
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents use highly technical, sometimes self-defined vocabulary and legal phrasing that can diverge from everyday language or field conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General LLMs trained on broad corpora may not capture self-defined or novel terms; domain-specific pretraining or fine-tuning on patent corpora and incorporating definitions is recommended. Distance-based embeddings and synonym heuristics can fail when terms are redefined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodality and role of drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents can include drawings/figures that complement textual descriptions; multimodal approaches can integrate text, images, and metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text is the primary legally binding carrier; drawings often are generic, low-resolution, or lack descriptive text and thus may be of limited standalone use. Hybrid models that combine text with image features and metadata (citations, classes) tend to perform better than image-only approaches. Dataset limitations (e.g., poor figure quality) and office rules limiting text in figures should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metadata usage for analysis and retrieval
rubrics_metrics.description: Metadata such as citations/references, classification codes, inventors, applicants, assignees, and examiners are valuable signals for retrieval, classification, valuation, and graph-based methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations naturally indicate relationships and can augment text embeddings; classification codes ease search but can be coarse and misleading for cross-domain inventions. Combining text embeddings with citation/knowledge-graph embeddings can improve performance (example: ~6% gain reported).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset curation and preprocessing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprocessing typically involves segmenting patents into sections (abstract, claims, description), rectifying irregularities (missing fields, encoding/format issues), and assembling task-specific labeled sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent offices provide raw bulk data but not always pre-processed structured datasets. Curated datasets (e.g., HUPD, BigPatent, DeepPatent) reduce effort. Researchers must handle paywalls, access restrictions, and decide on silver vs gold labeling approaches for tasks like simplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling heuristics and dataset caveats (novelty, simplification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some datasets use proxy heuristics for labels: e.g., novelty labeled by awards or cross-office rejection patterns; simplification datasets may be silver-standard generated by automatic tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These heuristics may not align with formal legal definitions (e.g., novelty) and can introduce bias. Gold-standard human annotations for tasks like simplification are expensive; researchers should report labeling method limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task taxonomy for patent NLP
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-related tasks are grouped into analysis (subject classification, retrieval, information extraction, novelty/granting/litigation prediction, valuation, forecasting, innovation recommendation) and generation (summarization, translation, simplification, patent writing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define task-specific datasets, baselines, and metrics. Note differences between tasks that use short text portions (title/abstract) and those that require full descriptions or claims; tailor model architectures and evaluation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification evaluation metrics and aggregation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Common classification metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. Aggregation across classes uses macro-averaging (equal weight per class) or micro-averaging (weight by class frequency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose macro vs micro based on class balance and evaluation goals; micro-averaging is often preferred when class imbalance exists. Formulas and definitions are provided (TP, TN, FP, FN).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information retrieval evaluation metrics (MAP, PRES, precision/recall)
rubrics_metrics.description: IR metrics include precision, recall, mean average precision (MAP), and domain-specific PRES (patent retrieval evaluation score) that measures rank deviation of relevant docs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MAP captures ranking quality across queries; PRES is tailored to patent retrieval to normalize rank deviations. Define relevant set sizes (NR, NK) carefully for patent collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-generation evaluation methods (human and automatic metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate generated patent text with human evaluation (gold standard) and automatic metrics: BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore; task-specific frameworks like PatentEval (error categorization) and keystroke-savings metrics have been proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human evaluation assesses accuracy, fluency, coherence, relevance but is costly. BLEU focuses on n-gram precision and literal matches; ROUGE prioritizes recall and suits summarization; METEOR accounts for stems/synonyms and balances precision/recall; BERTScore uses contextual embeddings to capture semantics. PatentEval categorizes generation errors (grammatical, irrelevant, incomplete, clarity). Use multiple metrics and human checks for legal-domain generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model selection guidance (general LLMs vs patent-specific models)
rubrics_metrics.description: General-purpose LLMs show strong capabilities but may be underdeveloped for patents; patent-specific LLMs and law-specific LLMs may better handle domain idiosyncrasies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider domain-specific pretraining or fine-tuning (PatentGPT, PatentGPT-J) and evaluate on curated patent tasks. Also consider long-context LLMs (models supporting 32k–128k tokens) when processing full descriptions. Report dataset provenance and model limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal modelling considerations and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: While multimodal models (text+image) can leverage complementary strengths, patent drawings are often generic or low-quality and textual elements remain primary for legal content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop multimodal datasets carefully (e.g., DeepPatent, IMPACT, PatentDesc) and be aware that many drawings lack descriptive text. Evaluate whether image signals add value per task; hybrid approaches generally preferred over image-only pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of citations and graph representations for downstream tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Graph-based methods leveraging citation links and classification relationships can support classification, valuation, and similarity detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations provide relational context; GNNs and combined text+graph embeddings can improve models. Be cautious that patent family and office-internal classifications may be coarser than needed for fine-grained technical similarity.
